messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Minh was forty-seven when the rupture happened at the downtown medical center where he was retrofitting a central ventilation system. He had been kneeling inside a narrow utility chase, wrench in hand, when a pressurized line of refrigerant and solvent vapor burst without warning. The cloud swallowed him instantly, thick and acrid, burning his throat and stinging his eyes. He remembered scrambling backward, his lungs seizing as he gagged on fumes that the site supervisor swore were temporary, but the panic that followed was anything but. When he finally crawled out onto the concrete pad, coughing until his ribs ached, the relief should have been immediate. Instead, a quiet dread settled into his bones. The smell of industrial cleaners, the sight of yellow caution tape, and the distant hum of a commercial compressor would later twist his stomach, but the memory that stayed sharp was the feeling of the vapor clinging to his skin long after he wiped himself down. Over the following months, Minh’s body refused to stand down. His shoulders remained permanently knotted, his breathing shallow and rapid the moment he stepped into any enclosed space. When his wife gently assured him that the air in their home was clean, or that a physician had confirmed no long-term lung damage, the words did nothing to quiet the vigilance humming under his skin. He had come to believe that safety was an illusion everyone else accepted but he could not. Even at home, his hands would automatically check the deadbolt, the window latches, and the utility room door until his fingers ached, as though securing the perimeter might keep whatever had happened from seeping back in. He told himself it was just being thorough, but deep down he knew it was the only way to keep the invisible threat from catching him off guard. Because his body remained locked in a state of constant readiness, Minh carved his days around staying off guard. When relaxation tried to creep in, he would feel a surge of dread so sharp it made his breath catch, so he deliberately kept busy, flipping through technical manuals or pacing the living room instead of resting. He stopped going to client homes alone, insisting his wife accompany him to every service call, and he began declining overtime or any job that required navigating tight mechanical rooms. What frightened him most was the loss of control, so he avoided anything that could stress his system, trading potential income for a predictable, tightly regulated routine. He told himself these boundaries were necessary, not because he was weakening, but because his nervous system was still reading the air for poison. His work as an HVAC technician, once a source of pride, became a landscape of quiet compromises. He still took calls, but he relegated himself to rooftop condensers and open mechanical floors where the air moved freely, avoiding the claustrophobic utility closets and sealed server rooms that mirrored the chase where he had nearly choked. When his foreman asked him to troubleshoot a complex multi-zone system in a downtown high-rise, Minh’s chest tightened so violently he had to step outside and lean against the brick wall until his pulse slowed. He told his boss he was taking a slower pace to focus on safety, but the truth was that the stress of diagnosing problems in confined, pressurized environments felt like stepping back into the cloud. The more he restricted his movements and the tasks he allowed himself to touch, the more his days narrowed, each avoided stressor simply becoming the next prerequisite for staying upright. It was his wife who finally pushed him to schedule an intake, noticing that he no longer slept through the night, that he flinched at the sound of his own toolkit being packed, and that his hands trembled while holding his coffee. At fifty-two, Minh was exhausted from the constant arithmetic of survival, from calculating which rooms, which tools, and which conversations were safe enough to endure. He had come to the clinic hoping someone could help him untangle the knot in his chest without taking the job he needed to keep their mortgage current, terrified that if he ever truly relaxed, the vapor would return and catch him before he could run.
